t: Subsequence of Size K With the Largest Even Sum — Greedy With Parity Repair
o: **Understanding the problem.** Only the sum matters, so a subsequence choice is really any size-k subset. Greedily taking the k largest works whenever their sum is even: for `[4,1,5,3,1]` with k = 3 that is {5, 4, 3} = 12. If the greedy sum is odd, we must trade one chosen element for an outside one of the opposite parity, losing as little as possible; when no such trade exists the answer is -1 — e.g. `[1,3,5]` with k = 1 has only odd singletons. Values reach $10^5$ and k can reach $10^5$, so sums reach $10^{10}$: 32-bit accumulators overflow and 64-bit integers are mandatory in C++/Java.
k: Order inside a subsequence is irrelevant — sort descending and reason about subsets.
A sum is even exactly when an even number of odd elements was chosen; parity is the whole difficulty.
If the greedy top-k sum is odd, swapping the smallest chosen element of one parity for the largest unchosen element of the other restores evenness at minimum loss.

a.n: Approach 1: Top-k Sum Plus One Parity Swap
a.i: Take the k largest; their sum S is optimal ignoring parity. If S is odd, the chosen set holds an odd number of odd values, and replacing exactly one element flips parity: either evict the smallest chosen odd for the largest unchosen even, or evict the smallest chosen even for the largest unchosen odd. Try both repairs, keep the better; if neither applies, return -1.
s: Sort nums descending; compute S = sum of the first k values.
If S is even, return S.
Search the chosen suffix for the smallest chosen odd and the outside prefix for the largest unchosen even; form the repaired sum if both exist.
Repeat symmetrically: smallest chosen even, largest unchosen odd.
Return the better valid repair, or -1.
a.t: O(n log n) — sorting dominates; the two swap searches are linear.

a.n: Approach 2: Parity Buckets With Prefix Sums
a.i: Enumerate j, the number of odds chosen, over even values only. The best selection with j odds takes the j largest odds plus the k-j largest evens, so prefix sums over each sorted bucket price every candidate in O(1). This sweeps all feasible parity splits exhaustively and is easy to prove correct.
s: Split nums into even and odd buckets, each sorted descending.
Build prefix sums preE and preO over the buckets.
Iterate j over 0, 2, 4, ... up to min(#odds, k).
Whenever k-j <= #evens, candidate = preO[j] + preE[k-j]; track the maximum.
Return the maximum candidate, or -1 if no split was feasible.
a.t: O(n log n) — the two bucket sorts dominate; the sweep is linear.
a.sp: O(n) — the buckets and their prefix arrays.

w: Approach 2 is the easiest to justify (every even number of odds tried), Approach 1 the fastest to whiteboard; both pass comfortably. Pitfalls: returning the raw top-k sum without a parity check; considering only one swap direction (both may be impossible, hence -1); stepping j over every integer instead of even ones; 32-bit overflow in C++/Java. Follow-ups: largest odd sum of size k, or the best even sum using at most k elements.
